To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the direct multiple sphere superposition simulations of the extinction of light in a random medium of spherical particles are in good agreement with effective medium theory and with measurements.

the extinction in random media can be described by the microphysical radiance theory and that the extinction in the diffusion regime is consistent with the diffusion approximation of radiative transfer.

the coherent field in a slab of randomly positioned spherical scatterers decays exponentially, that the effective attenuation coefficient of a random medium can be computed by a simple plane wave transmission and reflectivity model, and that the diffuse field is consistent with the diffusion approximation of radiative transfer theory.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a direct simulation of the extinction of light by a layer of spherical particles.
the development of a numerical methodology to simulate the radiative transport in a slab of randomly positioned spherical particles.
a detailed study of the coherent and inelastic components of the radiative field inside a slab of nonabsorbing particles.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the direct simulation of extinction in a slab of spherical particles is in excellent agreement with the radiative transfer theories and the effective medium theories.

direct simulation results for the coherent field are consistent with the microphysical theory of radiative transfer, while the diffuse flux results are consistent with the diffusion approximation to radiative transfer.
direct simulations, in the present form and with the present level of detail, provide the best possible test for the validity of the microphysical theory.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the results of our direct simulations of extinction in a slab of spheres are consistent with the predictions of the radiative transport theory and with the predictions of an effective medium theory.
we have shown that the direct multiple sphere superposition approach can be used to simulate the radiative transport properties of a random medium of spheres.

we have developed a new method for calculating the spatially dependent coherent and diffuse fields and energy flux in systems of randomly distributed nonabsorbing spheres and that the method can be used to test the validity of effective medium theories and to study the characteristics of the diffuse field and energy flux in particulate layers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the direct simulations of random media are an effective and accurate tool for testing and developing the theoretical models of extinction and diffusion in random media.
the coherent electric field and the energy flux are spatially dependent and that these quantities can be accurately computed from direct simulations.

the coherent and inelastic components to the electric field and Poyntings vector can be calculated exactly for systems of randomly positioned spheres and can thereby serve as a basis for a rigorous validation of the microphysical theory of radiative transfer.
